title: Git beyond the three commands: log, diff, rebase, cherry pick, bisect
story:
Git was begun by Linus Torvalds in April 2005, after the Linux kernel project lost free use of the proprietary system it had been relying on. The goals stated at the time are worth listing, because the tool's shape follows from them directly: speed, simple design, strong support for non-linear development with many parallel branches, full distribution so that every copy is a complete repository, and the ability to handle large projects efficiently.

Most confusion about the tool dissolves once the data model is clear, and the model is smaller than the command set implies.

Content is stored as objects addressed by a hash of the content itself. Two consequences follow immediately. Identical content is stored once, however many places it appears. And an identifier for an object is a verification of it — if the content changed, the identifier would not match, so the name and the integrity check are the same string.

A commit records a complete snapshot of the tree together with a pointer to its parent or parents. Note snapshot rather than change: the differences you see are computed by comparing two snapshots, not stored. And note parents, plural, which is what makes the history a directed acyclic graph rather than a sequence.

From which the thing everyone finds surprising follows without further explanation. A branch is not a copy of anything. It is a file containing the identifier of one commit. Creating a branch writes a few dozen bytes; deleting one removes them. Branching is cheap not as an optimisation but because there was never anything to copy, and any mental model in which branches are expensive is a model of a different tool.

The commands worth knowing beyond the basic three are the ones that use the graph rather than just extending it.

Examining differences between any two points is the foundation, since everything else is a question about what changed between which two commits. Taking one commit and applying it somewhere else is useful when a fix belongs on a release line as well as the main one. Replaying a series of commits onto a different base produces a linear history instead of a merge, which is a decision about legibility rather than correctness.

The one with the highest ratio of value to familiarity is the automated search for the commit that introduced a problem. Because history is a graph of snapshots, the tool can check out a commit halfway between a known-good and a known-bad point, wait for you to say which it is, and halve the remaining range. Finding the guilty commit among a thousand takes about ten tests rather than a thousand. It converts the question who broke this from an act of memory into a mechanical procedure — and it can be scripted, so the whole search runs unattended if the fault has an automatic test.

The cost of this design should be stated plainly, because it explains why the tool has a reputation for being frightening. The model is exposed rather than hidden. Commands that move pointers can be used to abandon commits, and the command set does not distinguish clearly between rearranging history that only you have and rearranging history that others have already built on. The first is routine and the second is destructive, and the difference is not in the command but in a fact about other people that the tool cannot see.

Which gives the only rule that reliably prevents disaster: before rewriting history, establish whether anyone else has the commits being rewritten. If they have, their work now descends from commits that no longer exist. Almost everything recoverable is recoverable because objects are kept until collected, so the mistake is usually reversible — but it is reversible by someone who knows the model, which is the argument for learning it rather than memorising commands.

problem.name: A graph of snapshots
problem.shape: A project's history must be inspected, searched, or rearranged.

branches are avoided because they feel expensive

recovery from a mistake means cloning a fresh copy
problem.move: Work from the model: commits are snapshots with parent pointers, and a branch is a file holding one identifier. Use the graph — search it automatically for the commit that introduced a fault rather than reasoning about it — and before rewriting history, establish whether anyone else has the commits involved.

cost.time: learning the model rather than a sequence of commands, which is more work up front and the only thing that makes recovery possible
cost.space: every copy holds the entire history, which is the price of every copy being a complete repository
cost.beats: a central system where history is a sequence, which is simpler and makes branching expensive and the server a single point of failure, and copying directories by hand, which needs no model and loses every relationship between versions

worked.problem: Why is creating a branch cheap, and what makes rewriting history dangerous?
worked.reasoning:
Both answers come out of the data model, which is smaller than the command set suggests.

Content is stored as objects addressed by a hash of the content itself. So identical content is stored once however often it appears, and an identifier is simultaneously a verification — if the content changed the identifier would not match, which means the name and the integrity check are the same string.

A commit records a complete snapshot of the tree plus a pointer to its parent or parents. Snapshot, not change: the differences displayed are computed by comparing two snapshots rather than stored. And parents in the plural, which is what makes history a directed acyclic graph rather than a sequence.

Branching follows without further explanation. A branch is not a copy of anything — it is a file containing the identifier of one commit. Creating one writes a few dozen bytes. So branching is not cheap as an optimisation; there was never anything to copy, and any mental model in which branches are expensive is a model of a different tool.

Rewriting is dangerous for a reason that is not in the commands at all. Operations that replay or reorder commits produce new commits — new snapshots with new parents and therefore new identifiers — and move a pointer to them. The old commits are not modified, because nothing is ever modified; they are simply no longer referenced.

That is harmless if the only reference was yours. It is destructive if someone else has those commits, because their work now descends from commits that no longer exist in your version of the history, and reconciling that is manual. The command is identical in both cases. The difference is a fact about other people that the tool cannot observe, which is why the rule has to be a habit rather than a safeguard: before rewriting, establish whether anyone else has the commits involved.

The recovery position is worth knowing and is more forgiving than the reputation suggests. Objects are kept until collected, so commits that became unreferenced usually still exist and can be recovered by someone who understands the model — which is the practical argument for learning the model rather than memorising commands.

The capability I would raise unprompted is the automated search for the commit that introduced a fault. Because history is a graph of snapshots, the tool can check out a commit halfway between a known-good and a known-bad point, take your verdict, and halve the remaining range. Among a thousand commits that is roughly ten tests rather than a thousand, and it converts who broke this from an act of memory into a mechanical procedure — scriptable, so the whole search runs unattended where the fault has an automatic test. It is the highest-value thing in the tool relative to how rarely it is used.

problem.practice: Take a bug whose introduction point you do not know and run the automated search for it against a known-good commit. Then check how many tests it took compared with the number of commits in the range.

beats.broke: Version control was a record of changes held centrally, so history was a sequence, branching was expensive, and an unreachable server was a lost project.
beats.fix: Address content by a hash of itself and record each commit as a snapshot with pointers to its parents — which makes a branch one small file and gives every copy the entire history.
beats.cost: The model is exposed rather than hidden, and the command set does not distinguish rearranging history only you hold from rearranging history others have built on.

interview.q: Why is creating a branch cheap, and what makes rewriting history dangerous?
interview.trap: Explaining branch cheapness as an optimisation. There is nothing to copy — a branch is a file holding one commit identifier, so the cost was never there to optimise away.
interview.answer:
Both come out of the data model, which is smaller than the command set suggests.

Content is stored as objects addressed by a hash of the content itself, so identical content is stored once and an identifier is simultaneously a verification — if the content changed, the identifier would not match, so the name and the integrity check are the same string.

A commit records a complete snapshot of the tree plus a pointer to its parent or parents. Snapshot, not change: displayed differences are computed by comparing two snapshots rather than stored. Parents in the plural is what makes history a directed acyclic graph rather than a sequence.

So branching follows: a branch is not a copy of anything, it is a file containing one commit's identifier. Creating one writes a few dozen bytes. It is not cheap as an optimisation — there was never anything to copy, and a mental model in which branches are expensive is a model of a different tool.

Rewriting is dangerous for a reason not in the commands. Replaying or reordering produces new commits — new snapshots, new parents, new identifiers — and moves a pointer to them. The old commits are not modified, because nothing is ever modified; they are just no longer referenced. That is harmless if the only reference was yours and destructive if someone else has them, because their work now descends from commits that no longer exist in your history. The command is identical in both cases, and the difference is a fact about other people the tool cannot observe — which is why the rule has to be a habit: establish who else has the commits before rewriting.

Recovery is more forgiving than the reputation suggests, since objects are kept until collected, so unreferenced commits usually still exist — recoverable by someone who understands the model, which is the argument for learning it rather than memorising commands.

The capability I would raise unprompted is the automated search for the commit that introduced a fault: the tool checks out a commit halfway between known-good and known-bad, takes your verdict, and halves the range. Among a thousand commits that is about ten tests, and it converts 'who broke this' from memory into a mechanical, scriptable procedure.
